source.anchor: Proof first paragraph and first display

nodes.content: There exists g_t in partial ell_t(x_t) such that <eta_t g_t + grad psi(x_t)-grad psi(x_{t-1}), u-x_t> >= 0 for all u in V. The source attributes this to Theorem 2.8.
nodes.validity: Unresolved application gap G-optimality; existence of some subgradient alone does not supply this selected subgradient.

source.anchor: Proof Hence display, first inequality

nodes.content: eta_t(ell_t(x_t)-ell_t(u)) <= <eta_t g_t,x_t-u>; from global supporting inequality and eta_t>0.

source.anchor: Proof Hence display, second inequality

nodes.content: <eta_t g_t,x_t-u> <= <grad psi(x_{t-1})-grad psi(x_t),x_t-u>; rearranges P-optimality.

source.anchor: Proof Hence display, final equality; attribution continued on PDF278

nodes.content: <grad psi(x_{t-1})-grad psi(x_t),x_t-u> = B(u;x_{t-1})-B(u;x_t)-B(x_t;x_{t-1}). Lemma 6.7 uses (x,y,z)=(x_t,x_{t-1},u), then negates both sides.

source.anchor: Entire Hence display

nodes.content: eta_t(ell_t(x_t)-ell_t(u)) <= B(u;x_{t-1})-B(u;x_t)-B(x_t;x_{t-1}).

source.anchor: Proof continuation first sentence and first line of display

nodes.content: Divide by eta_t>0 and sum t=1,...,T: R_T <= sum_t [B(u;x_{t-1})/eta_t-B(u;x_t)/eta_t] - sum_t B(x_t;x_{t-1})/eta_t.

source.anchor: Proof continuation display, second line equality

nodes.content: Weighted difference sum = B(u;x_0)/eta_1 - B(u;x_T)/eta_T + sum_{t=1}^{T-1}(1/eta_{t+1}-1/eta_t)B(u;x_t); the negative movement sum remains unchanged. This is an equality of RHS expressions, not an equality with regret.

source.anchor: where we denoted paragraph

nodes.content: D^2=max_{0<=s<=T-1} B(u;x_s). The previous states, including x_0 and excluding x_T, are the bounded positive-coefficient terms.

source.anchor: Proof continuation display, third line inequality

nodes.content: Use eta_{t+1}<=eta_t and positivity for nonnegative inverse-step increments; bound B(u;x_0) and B(u;x_t), t=1,...,T-1, by D^2; drop -B(u;x_T)/eta_T <=0. Retain -sum_t B(x_t;x_{t-1})/eta_t.

source.anchor: Proof continuation display, fourth line equality

nodes.content: D^2/eta_1 + D^2 sum_{t=1}^{T-1}(1/eta_{t+1}-1/eta_t) = D^2/eta_1 + D^2(1/eta_T-1/eta_1); movement sum unchanged.

source.anchor: Proof continuation display, final line equality

nodes.content: D^2/eta_1+D^2(1/eta_T-1/eta_1) = D^2/eta_T; movement sum unchanged.

source.anchor: Sentence The second statement is left as an exercise

source.anchor: Definition 2.16

nodes.content: A function f:R^d -> [-infinity,+infinity] is closed iff every real sublevel set {x:f(x)<=alpha} is closed.

source.anchor: Definition 2.18

nodes.content: Proper means nowhere -infinity and finite somewhere; losses satisfy this through nonempty V subset dom ell_t.

source.anchor: Definition 2.20; continuation PDF29 first two paragraphs

nodes.content: For proper f, g in partial f(x) means f(y)>=f(x)+<g,y-x> for every y in R^d; partial f(x) is the set, subdifferentiability means it is nonempty. For proper convex f, dom partial f subset dom f.

source.anchor: Definition 6.3

nodes.content: Strict convexity on convex V: f(alpha x+(1-alpha)y)<alpha f(x)+(1-alpha)f(y) for distinct x,y and 0<alpha<1.

source.anchor: Definition 6.4

nodes.content: Strictly convex psi:X->R, differentiable on nonempty int X. B_psi:X x int X -> R, B(a;b)=psi(a)-psi(b)-<grad psi(b),a-b>. The opening sentence on PDF76 names psi the distance generating function associated to B_psi.

source_continuation.anchor: First sentence: function psi associated to B_psi is called the distance generating function

source.anchor: Opening paragraph after distance generating function sentence

nodes.content: For fixed y in int X, psi(x)>=psi(y)+<grad psi(y),x-y> for all x in X, equality only at x=y. Thus B(x;y)>=0 including boundary x; not merely for x in int X.
nodes.retained_scope: Only supporting inequality, nonnegativity and equality case; reference-dependent similarity and lack of symmetry are explicitly excluded in X76-reference-dependence and X76-nonsymmetry.

source.anchor: Paragraph between Definitions 6.3 and 6.4

nodes.content: Differentiable strictly convex functions satisfy strict tangent inequality for distinct points; attributed to Bauschke and Combettes (2017), Proposition 17.10. The neighboring strong-convexity observation is separately excluded.

source.anchor: Lemma 6.7

nodes.content: For x,y in int X and z in X: B(z;x)+B(x;y)-B(z;y)=<grad psi(y)-grad psi(x),z-x>. No proof paragraph printed here; attributed to Chen and Teboulle (1993).

source.anchor: References entry G. Chen and M. Teboulle

nodes.content: Convergence analysis of a proximal-like minimization algorithm using Bregman functions. SIAM Journal on Optimization, 3(3):538-543, 1993. External work itself not inspected; book identity is inspected.

source.anchor: Theorem 2.8

nodes.content: V nonempty convex, x* in V, f convex and differentiable on an open set containing V: x* in argmin_V f iff <grad f(x*),y-x*> >=0 for all y in V.

source.anchor: Theorem 2.8 proof first paragraph and display

nodes.content: From Theorem2.7 and nonnegative feasible directional inner products, f(y)>=f(x*)+<grad f(x*),y-x*> >= f(x*) for every y in V.

source.anchor: Theorem 2.8 proof second paragraph

nodes.content: If a feasible y has negative directional inner product, z(alpha)=alpha y+(1-alpha)x* remains feasible; h(alpha)=f(z(alpha)) has h'(0)<0. By derivative definition a small positive alpha gives f(z(alpha))<f(x*), contradiction.

source.anchor: Theorem 2.7

nodes.content: For convex f:R^d->(-infinity,+infinity], x in int dom f, differentiability at x gives f(y)>=f(x)+<grad f(x),y-x> for all y. Cites Rockafellar (1970), Theorem25.1 and Corollary25.1.1.

source.anchor: Proof first sentence invoking Theorem2.8

nodes.content: The cited theorem requires a differentiable objective on an open neighborhood of all V. The update objective includes a merely subdifferentiable ell_t; psi is differentiable only on int X and V may meet boundary X. No printed nonsmooth sum/normal-cone bridge supplies the claimed selected g_t. Source does not assert ell_t closed. Do not import equality sum-rule hypotheses as theorem binders.
